note: The representative of the Aristotelian falāsifa whom the Khazar king consults first. His self-sufficient, impersonal God frames the entire dialogue — and is the first position HaLevi sets out to refute.

In the philosopher's Aristotelian-Neoplatonic scheme, the ultimate source from which all existence flows by necessity (emanation), not by will or purpose. HaLevi voices this doctrine in order to attack it.
A synonym here for the First Cause — the apex of the causal chain. To say God 'created' a person is, for the philosopher, only loose speech: He is the remote Cause of causes, not a purposive Creator.
The philosopher holds the world is qadīm — eternal — against the doctrine of creation in time. A central point of dispute throughout the Kuzari.
Particular, changing things. The philosophers deny that God knows them, since His knowledge admits no change — so, they argue, He cannot know your intentions or hear your prayer.
To say God 'created you' is, for the philosopher, only majāz (figurative) — He is the Cause of causes, not a Maker who intended you specifically.
The lowest of the separate intellects in Arabic Aristotelian cosmology. The perfected human intellect 'conjoins' with it — the summit of the philosopher's ideal of human perfection.
The human intellect in potential, also called al-ʿaql al-hayūlānī ('material'). Actualized through learning until it conjoins with the Active Intellect.
The goal of the philosopher's path: the passive intellect joins the Active Intellect in a union (ittiṣāl ittiḥād) so complete that one no longer distinguishes the two.
